analysis.one_liner: Extends by ten years the patent on one cancer-treatment drug, Ethiofos.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee and died at the end of the 102nd Congress, so the patent expired on schedule.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a private bill, written for a single company: it told the Commerce Department to add ten extra years to one specific patent, number 3,892,824, covering the drug Ethiofos (WR2721) and its oral form. A patent gives its owner the exclusive right to sell a drug, so a ten-year extension means ten more years without cheaper generic competition. Rep. Mike Synar introduced it "by request," which means he filed it at the request of an outside party, with no cosponsors. The House Judiciary Committee referred it to a subcommittee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The holder of the named patent, who would keep exclusive rights to sell Ethiofos for a decade past the normal expiration, allowing continued premium pricing without generic competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The holder of one drug patent

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Commerce to extend United States Patent Number 3,892,824 for ten years "with all the rights pertaining thereto" once it expires, preserving the patent holder's exclusive right to sell Ethiofos and its oral analogue [S3].
It is a private bill benefiting one named patent; the CRS summary simply directs Commerce to extend "a certain numbered patent" by ten years [S2].
The bill was introduced "by request" on behalf of an outside party, a routine device for filing legislation at a requester's behest [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients who use the drug, and the insurers and programs paying for it, would face higher prices for ten additional years because a cheaper generic version could not enter. Supporters would argue the extension compensates a developer for years the patent was eaten up by drug testing and approval, and rewards the investment that brought the drug to patients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients and insurers buying the drug

drawbacks.text: A ten-year patent extension blocks generic competition for that decade, keeping the drug's price above the cheaper generic level for patients and payers [S3].
The bill is drafted for one specific patent number rather than a general rule, so its benefit goes to a single company rather than to drug developers as a class [S3].

An honest supporter would concede that special patent extensions for individual drugs are a slower, case-by-case substitute for the general law that already compensates for patent time lost to regulatory review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs almost entirely to one patent holder; the cost is spread thinly but broadly across everyone who pays for the drug over ten extra years of exclusivity. Whatever the developer's justification, a one-company patent extension is a poor way to weigh that trade-off, because it bypasses any general debate about patent terms. In any case, the choice never had to be made: the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to an intellectual property subcommittee, which never acted, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Synar introduced the bill on March 6, 1991, by request, and it was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
On March 14, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors [S4] and never received a committee markup, a floor vote in either chamber, or a signature [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients, insurers, and future generic drug makers are better off, because the drug's patent expired on schedule and prices could fall once generics entered.

for.name: Rep. Mike Synar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the patent-extension bill on behalf of an outside requester and saw it referred to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to a subcommittee, then took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill or scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have given one company ten extra years of exclusive sales rights on Ethiofos, keeping its price above the generic level. The gain is the public's cost, borne by patients and insurers over that decade.
A ten-year extension would have kept generics off the market for the drug for a decade. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran alongside patients' interest in lower prices.
